why_this_block_exists: Validate is a sequential finding-validation workflow: one fast coding pass
checks the finding narrative for hallucinated claims, then one slow coding pass
does reachability/latency research and writes the same summary/severity artifacts
as triage. It intentionally has no lenses.

title: Validate a kres finding against a source workspace
description: Research a kres finding with false-positive elimination as the explicit goal: validate the finding's claims against source with typed provenance, test whether the surviving preconditions can hold simultaneously, prove reachability or non-latency, write summary.md, and synchronize severity in metadata.yaml and FINDING.md.

target.description: Absolute path to a kres finding directory (must contain FINDING.md and metadata.yaml).

source_workspace.description: Source workspace used for source, grep, git, semcode, and auto skill selection. The /validate command defaults this to the active workspace.

slow_secondary_available.description: Machine-populated. True when the session has a second slow model configured (settings.models.slow_secondary, or a second --slow selection). Guards the secondary refutation step: without it that step would re-run the primary model and call it independent.

steps.title: Validate finding claims against source
prompt: Finding directory: {{workflow.target}}
Source workspace: {{workflow.source_workspace}}
Read the finding's metadata.yaml and FINDING.md. Validate the factual
statements made in the finding against the source workspace. Treat false
positive elimination as the goal: verify cited files, functions, line
claims, call paths, locking/context claims, return-value assumptions,
configuration assumptions, and impact claims. Use source/grep/callers/git
followups when the supplied finding text is not enough.
Use bounded git commands for commit-status questions. If metadata, prior
results, or finding text cites a fixing or introducing commit, do not ask
for `git log <sha>` because that dumps the entire ancestry reachable from
the commit. Use `git show -s --oneline <sha>` to check that a commit object
exists, and `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD` to check whether that
commit is present in the source workspace's current HEAD. Use `git log -1`
or path/pickaxe-limited history only when you need one bounded commit or a
specific bounded history search.
Do not update files in this step. Do not triage severity in this step.
Do not use or simulate parallel lenses. Produce structured outputs only;
do not rely on prose as a hidden control channel.
State the finding's `thesis` in one sentence: what it claims is broken.
The next step tests whether your claims can all hold at once against
that thesis, so write it as the specific defect, not the subsystem.
Then emit one `claims` entry per material statement. Four fields decide
what happens downstream, so get them right:
- `kind`. A `precondition` is a claim of the form "this only happens
when X" — a config, a runtime state, a lock being held or not held, a
return value, a caller. Those are what the conjunction step compares.
`mechanism` is how the defect works, `reachability` is who can reach
it, `impact` is what it costs, `design_intent` is evidence the
behaviour is deliberate.
- `verdict`. `supported` needs evidence. `contradicted` needs evidence
and a `correction`. `unresolved` needs `source_needed` naming exactly
what would settle it. If the finding is only valid when a function can
return NULL, sleep, drop a reference, or skip initialization, check
that precondition or mark it unresolved.
- `gating`. True when the bug does not exist if the claim is false.
Frequency, severity, fix strategy and "how bad is it" are NOT gating.
A gating claim left unresolved caps the final verdict; this field is
read by Rust, not by a later model.
- `evidence[].provenance`. `fresh` means you fetched it this session
through source/read/grep/callers/git. `finding_quoted` means it is
only present as text pasted inside FINDING.md or metadata.yaml. A
gating claim supported solely by the finding quoting itself has
verified nothing, and this step will be rejected and re-run. Fetch the
definition instead.
`design_intent` is required. Before deciding a behaviour is a defect,
look for evidence its author intended it: the leading comment on the
function or type, an enumerated design table or rank ordering nearby,
or the introducing commit's message. Set `checked` true once you have
looked, and put what you found in `evidence` (with file:line or sha) or
null if there was none. If a fetched definition arrives with no leading
comment, read the ~15 lines above it before concluding there is none.

analysis.description: Brief narrative of the claim-validation work.

thesis.description: One sentence: what the finding claims is broken. The conjunction step tests the claims against this.

id.description: Short stable slug, unique within this report.

gating.description: True when the bug does not exist if this claim is false. Severity, frequency and fix-strategy claims are not gating.

location.description: file:line, commit sha, or search expression the evidence came from.

provenance.description: fresh = fetched this session via source/read/grep/callers/git. finding_quoted = only present as text inside FINDING.md or metadata.yaml.

correction.description: For contradicted claims: what the finding should say instead.

source_needed.description: For unresolved claims: the exact source, history or search that would settle it.

checked.description: True once you have actually looked for evidence that the behaviour is intended.

evidence.description: The comment, enumerated design table, or introducing-commit text showing the behaviour is intended, with its file:line or sha. Null when you looked and found none.

citation_check.description: Machine-populated. Resolves each file:line citation against the workspace and confirms every `fresh` citation names a file the fetcher actually delivered. Not emitted by the model.

followups.description: Typed source/history/context requests needed before the slow validation pass.

steps.title: Can every supported precondition hold at once?
prompt: Finding thesis: {{validate-claims.claim_validation.thesis}}
Claim report from the validation pass:
{{validate-claims.claim_validation}}
You have exactly one job. Every claim above was checked on its own.
Nobody has yet asked whether they can all be true of the SAME
execution. Ask that.
Findings die here that survive everywhere else. A report can state
"this path cannot run when core scheduling is active" and, four
entries later, "the reader of that state exists only when core
scheduling is compiled in and enabled" — each claim correct, the
conjunction empty, the finding impossible. That is the single largest
class of false positive this workflow has shipped.
Compare the preconditions pairwise. Emit a `conflicts` entry for each
pair that cannot hold together, naming both claim ids and why.
Then try to build `single_execution_witness`: ONE configuration under
which every gating precondition holds simultaneously.
- `build_config` is compile-time only: kconfig symbols that must be
set. `runtime_state` is everything else — a static branch enabled, a
sysctl or debugfs value, a scheduler feature, a cgroup setting, a
hardware topology, a lock held or not held. These are different
conditions and merging them is how contradictory claims start to
look compatible: a kernel can have CONFIG_X=y while the runtime gate
X_enabled() is false, and in that state the code guarded by the
runtime gate is dormant.
- `call_site` is one concrete file:line where the defect executes with
all of the above true.
- `concurrent_writer` applies when the finding asserts a race. Name the
function that writes the racing state inside the window and say how
it runs concurrently — another CPU, an interrupt, a preemption point.
"The window is narrow but real" is not a writer. If the only writer
is the same task executing the window, or every writer is excluded by
a lock the window holds, there is no race: set this null.
Set `single_execution_witness` to null when no such configuration
exists, and say why in `witness_reasoning`. A null witness does not by
itself invalidate the finding — the next step decides that — but
inventing a witness to avoid emitting null does.
You may fetch source to settle a specific compatibility question. Do
not re-validate the claims; that already happened.

analysis.description: Brief narrative of the satisfiability reasoning.

consistent.description: True when every supported precondition can hold simultaneously.

why.description: Why the two cannot both hold on one execution.

build_config.description: Kconfig symbols that must be set, e.g. CONFIG_SCHED_CORE=y. Compile-time only.

runtime_state.description: Runtime conditions that must hold, e.g. sched_core_enabled(rq) == true, a static branch enabled, a sysctl, a cgroup setting, a topology. NOT kconfig.

call_site.description: file:line of one concrete site where the defect executes under the above.

concurrent_writer.description: For a race: the function that writes the racing state, and how it runs concurrently (other CPU, interrupt, preemption). Null for a non-race defect, or when no such writer could be named.

witness_reasoning.description: How the witness was assembled, or why no witness exists.

conjunction.description: Pairwise conflicts and the single-execution witness.

followups.description: Typed requests for source needed to settle a compatibility question.

steps.title: Prove reachability and write validated triage
prompt: {{workflow.target}}
Source workspace: {{workflow.source_workspace}}
Validate the kres finding at the absolute path on the first line. Apply
the embedded triage template (see INCLUDES) for summary.md formatting,
status selection, severity selection, metadata.yaml updates, FINDING.md
header updates, and triage_coding output. This is stricter than ordinary
triage: the explicit goal is to eliminate false positives.
The claim-validation pass produced this structured report:
{{validate-claims.claim_validation}}
The conjunction pass produced this satisfiability report:
{{validate-conjunction.conjunction}}
Use both as a checklist, then close every material open question that
gates whether the bug exists. If the finding is only valid when function
A returns NULL, prove whether function A can return NULL on the relevant
path. If the finding depends on context, locking, lifetime,
configuration, caller reachability, privilege, or a specific return value,
trace the source until that precondition is supported or contradicted.
Use bounded git commands for commit-status questions. If metadata, prior
results, or finding text cites a fixing or introducing commit, do not ask
for `git log <sha>` because that dumps the entire ancestry reachable from
the commit. Use `git show -s --oneline <sha>` to check that a commit object
exists, and `git merge-base --is-ancestor <sha> HEAD` to check whether that
commit is present in the source workspace's current HEAD. Use `git log -1`
or path/pickaxe-limited history only when you need one bounded commit or a
specific bounded history search.
A valid summary must be evidence based, and false-positive elimination is
the explicit goal. Use the status decision tree in the embedded triage
template (it defines Invalid, Not A Defect, Confirmed Latent, Unconfirmed,
Plausible, Fixed, and Unknown), but apply it more strictly:
- Do not preserve a finding as Plausible when any load-bearing component
remains unresolved.
- Unconfirmed is only for a bug-existence gate that is still genuinely open —
one you could neither prove nor disprove. Do NOT use Unconfirmed for a
gate you actually resolved negatively.
- If you proved the defect cannot exist as described, that is Invalid. If
the behaviour does occur but source evidence shows it is what the author
intended, that is NotADefect. If you proved the defect structure is real
but 100% of the finding has no current in-tree trigger, that is Confirmed
Latent (verdict `ConfirmedLatent`), not Unconfirmed — follow the
template's Confirmed Latent handling for status, reachability, and
triage_coding tagging.
A finding is latent-only only when every component lacks a current in-tree
trigger; if ANY component is currently reachable and valid, keep the finding
valid and explain the reachable component instead of downgrading the whole
finding.
Three of those decisions are checked by Rust after you answer, not by
another model, so answer them in the typed fields rather than in prose:
- A gating claim the first pass left `unresolved` caps this finding below
Plausible. To keep it Plausible you must settle the claim here and say
so in `gating_override`, with file:line evidence. Re-describing the
claim as a probability, frequency, severity or triggerability question
is not settling it, and is the specific move this check exists to stop.
- Every pair in the conjunction step's `conflicts` caps this finding below
Plausible until you address it in `conflict_resolution`.
- A null `single_execution_witness` means nobody could name one
configuration where the finding fires. Plausible requires one.
If you cannot supply those, the honest verdict is Invalid, NotADefect,
ConfirmedLatent or Unconfirmed, and choosing one of those is not a
failure of the run.
Do not use or simulate parallel lenses. Emit `summary.md`,
`metadata.yaml`, and `FINDING.md` as absolute-path code_output entries
under the finding directory. Rewrite stale open questions, reproducers,
and original-finding body text that your validation contradicted; do not
leave `metadata.yaml` or `FINDING.md` saying the old question remains open
after you have closed it in `summary.md`.
When writing metadata.yaml, add or update this top-level marker exactly:
`validation_run: true`. This distinguishes validation output from ordinary
triage output for batch wrappers.
Return a `verdict` field in your structured outputs naming the chosen
human status exactly as one of: Fixed | Plausible | Unconfirmed | Unknown |
Invalid | ConfirmedLatent | NotADefect. Return a `severity` field exactly
as one of: high | medium | low.
Also return `triage_coding` as a structured object derived from the same
summary.md content you emit. Do not put this JSON inside summary.md. The
human `verdict` and machine `triage_coding.summary_status` intentionally
use different casing: if verdict is `Invalid`, summary_status must be
`invalid`; if verdict is `Unconfirmed`, summary_status must be
`unconfirmed`; if verdict is `ConfirmedLatent`, summary_status must be
`confirmed_latent`; if verdict is `NotADefect`, summary_status must be
`not_a_defect`.
Required `triage_coding` shape:
- schema_version: integer, set to 1
- severity: one of high, medium, low
- summary_status: one of fixed, plausible, unconfirmed, unknown, invalid, confirmed_latent, not_a_defect
- summary_subject: short subject string from the summary, or empty string
- impact_classes: array of lowercase strings such as local_dos, remote_dos, memory_corruption, privilege_escalation, info_leak, data_corruption, vm_escape, latent, test_only, unknown
- config_commonness: one of common, niche, debug_or_test_only, unknown

- reject_reasons: array of lowercase strings for reasons this should not enter a fix queue, such as invalid, unconfirmed, unknown_reachability, latent_only, intentional_design, test_only, niche_config, fixed_already

- reachability: object with host_access, remote_access, root_required, regular_user as yes/no/n/a/unknown strings, plus build_config {required, symbols[]} for compile-time gating and runtime_state {required, conditions[]} for everything that must additionally hold at run time. Keep those two apart: CONFIG_X=y and X_enabled() are different conditions.
- touches: object with files array and subsystems array, populated only from explicit summary text
- actionability: object with fix_queue_eligible boolean and rationale string
- priority: object with tier one of critical, high, medium, low, none, unknown; score integer 0-100; reason string
- evidence: object with status, impact, reachability, and actionability strings quoting or summarizing the summary text that supports the classification
Rust must be able to consume the JSON fields directly; do not hide routing,
status, or severity decisions in prose.
If this step is running again after a refutation, the refutations are
reproduced above under PRIOR REFUTATIONS. A refutation you do not
answer stands: either drop below Plausible, or answer it in
`refutation_rebuttal` with evidence. Restating the original claim more
firmly is not an answer.

severity.description: Severity assigned by validation and written to metadata.yaml, FINDING.md, and summary.md.

resolution.description: How both can hold on one execution after all, or which of the two is wrong.

evidence.description: file:line or commit evidence for the resolution.

conflict_resolution.description: Required to keep a finding Plausible when the conjunction step reported conflicts: one entry per conflicting pair.

evidence.description: file:line evidence that settles the claim. Not a re-argument.

gating_override.description: The only way to keep a finding Plausible when a gating claim was left unresolved: settle it here with evidence.

rebuttal.description: Why the refutation does not hold.

evidence.description: file:line, commit or search evidence for the rebuttal. Not a re-argument of the original claim.

refutation_rebuttal.description: Required to keep a finding Plausible after a refutation step broke it: one entry per successful refutation, each with evidence.

summary_written.description: Machine-populated. True only when this step emitted and wrote a non-empty summary.md.

severity_written.description: Machine-populated. True only when this step emitted summary.md, metadata.yaml, and FINDING.md and their persisted contents contain the chosen severity.

followups.description: Typed requests for missing source/type/history/context if the finding cannot be validated from the available evidence.

code_output.description: Files emitted by the validation step: summary.md, metadata.yaml, and FINDING.md.

symbols.description: Kconfig symbols that must be set, e.g. CONFIG_SCHED_CORE=y.

conditions.description: Static branches, sysctls, scheduler features, cgroup settings, topology — conditions that must hold at run time even when the build config is set.

runtime_state.description: Runtime gating. Distinct from build_config: a kernel can have CONFIG_X=y while X_enabled() is false.

triage_coding.description: Structured classification derived from the generated summary.md content.

steps.title: Try to break the finding (primary model)
prompt: Finding directory: {{workflow.target}}
Source workspace: {{workflow.source_workspace}}
A validation pass concluded this finding is a real, currently
reachable bug. Your job is to break it. You are not asked for a
balanced assessment and you are not the one who has to be fair to
the finding; the pass that just ran already made its case.
Verdict reached: {{validate-reachability.verdict}}
The summary it wrote:
{{validate-reachability.triage_coding}}
The claim report behind it:
{{validate-claims.claim_validation}}
The satisfiability report and the execution witness:
{{validate-conjunction.conjunction}}
Everything the run gathered is attached: the fetched symbols and
context are in this request. Work from those. Do not request more
source; nothing will fetch it, and the question is whether the
evidence already in hand actually supports the conclusion.
Six of eight false positives in a hand audit of a previous export
had the disproving fact already in the context you are being given,
and three had it written down as a supported claim. So read the
claims against each other and against the witness rather than
looking for something new:
- Can every precondition really hold at once, on one execution? A
compile-time gate and a runtime gate are different conditions.
- Does the witness describe a state the kernel can actually be in,
or is it a list of requirements nobody checked for compatibility?
- For a race: is the named concurrent writer real, and can it run
in the window? A writer that is the same task, or one excluded by
a lock the window already holds, is not a race.
- Is the behaviour intentional? A comment, a design table, or the
introducing commit saying so makes this not a defect.
- Does the impact follow, or does the mechanism stop short of it?
Set `refuted` true only when you can point at the thing that breaks
it, and put that in `decisive_evidence`. "I am not convinced" is
not a refutation: if the finding survives, say so and name the
claim it most depends on in `weakest_link`. A refutation you cannot
evidence sends the finding back for another expensive pass, so do
not bluff.

analysis.description: Brief narrative of the attempt to break the finding.

refuted.description: True when you can show the finding does not hold as written.

reasoning.description: The strongest case against the finding, whether or not it succeeded.

decisive_evidence.description: When refuted: the file:line, commit or search result that breaks it. Null otherwise.

weakest_link.description: The claim id or precondition the finding most depends on, even when you could not break it.

refutation.description: Whether the finding survives an attempt to break it.
